questions_json.explanation: Chronic stress raises cortisol, which weakens immune function. Research by Kiecolt-Glaser showed stressed caregivers heal wounds more slowly and respond weaker to vaccines.
options: Chronic stress suppresses her immune system, slowing healing
She is only imagining the slow healing
Colds are caused by cold weather alone
Caregiving has no effect on physical health
questions_json.q: Ayesha has been caring for her sick mother for two years with little rest. She catches every cold, and a small cut on her hand takes weeks to heal. What best explains this?

questions_json.explanation: Cohen's famous cold study showed people reporting the most stress were most likely to develop colds after virus exposure — stress weakens immune defenses.
options: Stress has no link to illness
Only viruses cause colds; stress is irrelevant
Higher stress increases vulnerability to infection
questions_json.q: In a well-known study, healthy volunteers were exposed to cold viruses. Those who reported the most stress in the past year were most likely to develop colds. What does this show?

questions_json.explanation: Problem-focused coping tackles the source of stress directly (Lazarus & Folkman). It works best when the situation can actually be changed.
questions_json.q: Bilal loses his job. He immediately updates his CV, contacts friends for referrals, and starts learning new skills. Which coping style is he using?

questions_json.explanation: Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings around stress. It fits situations that cannot be changed, like bereavement, where soothing emotions matters most.
questions_json.q: After her father's death, Sara talks to close friends, allows herself to cry, and slowly reframes the loss as a reminder to value family. Which coping style is this?

questions_json.explanation: The Health Belief Model says people take health action when they feel susceptible, see the illness as serious, and believe the benefits outweigh the barriers.
questions_json.q: A free diabetes screening camp gets few visitors. A health psychologist says people stayed away because they don't feel at risk and doubt the test helps. Which model is she using?

questions_json.explanation: Melzack and Wall's gate control theory: a 'gate' in the spinal cord can block pain signals when the brain is excited or focused — pain is psychological as well as physical.
options: Pain is purely a physical signal
He must have no pain receptors
Gate control theory — the brain can close the 'gate' on pain signals
questions_json.q: A footballer badly injures his ankle during a final match but feels almost no pain until the game ends. Which theory best explains this?

questions_json.explanation: Non-adherence is very common — about half of chronic-illness patients skip doses. Feeling no symptoms, high cost, and complex routines are top reasons.
options: Non-adherence — feeling fine and high cost are common barriers
questions_json.q: An elderly man stops taking his blood pressure pills because he 'feels fine' and the pills are expensive. What is this an example of?

questions_json.explanation: Social support buffers stress and aids recovery — supported patients show better immune function, faster healing, and even lower mortality after surgery.
options: The lonely patient will recover faster
Social support makes no difference to recovery
The supported patient is likely to recover faster with fewer complications
questions_json.q: Two women recover from the same surgery. One gets daily family visits; the other lives alone with no visitors. What does research predict?

questions_json.explanation: Friedman and Rosenman's Type A pattern — especially hostility and time urgency — is linked to higher heart disease risk. The toxic ingredient is anger, not mere busyness.
options: Hostility and time urgency (Type A behavior)
questions_json.q: A manager is always rushing, gets angry in traffic, and tries to do three things at once. Which trait raises his heart disease risk, according to Friedman and Rosenman?

questions_json.explanation: Lazarus's model: primary appraisal asks 'is this a threat?', secondary appraisal asks 'can I cope?' The same event stresses people differently based on these judgments.
options: Stress appraisal — how we judge a threat and our ability to cope
questions_json.q: Two students face the same difficult exam. One sees it as a challenge and studies calmly; the other sees it as a threat and panics. This difference is called:
